section.title: The Priestly Garments Completed
section.sectionRationale: The craftsmen finish the priestly garments exactly as commanded, the refrain 'just as the LORD had commanded Moses' repeating throughout, and every piece of the tabernacle is brought to Moses, who inspects it all and blesses the people for their faithful obedience.
section.thesis: The skilled workers complete the ephod, breastpiece, robe, and remaining priestly garments precisely as the LORD commanded, and when everything is brought to Moses, he inspects it all and blesses the people because they had done exactly as the LORD instructed.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the ephod and its memorial stones; the breastpiece of judgment with its gemstones; the robe and remaining garments; and everything brought to Moses, inspected, and found to match every command.

units.label: The ephod
units.note: just as the LORD had commanded Moses

media.alt: Finished priestly garments laid before a tent
media.caption: Every garment is finished exactly as the LORD had commanded Moses.

verses.text: From the blue, purple, and scarlet yarn they made specially woven garments for ministry in the sanctuary, as well as the holy garments for Aaron, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
Bezalel made the ephod of finely spun linen embroidered with gold, and with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn.
They hammered out thin sheets of gold and cut threads from them to interweave with the blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen, the work of a skilled craftsman.
They made shoulder pieces for the ephod, which were attached at two of its corners, so it could be fastened.

And the skillfully woven waistband of the ephod was of one piece with the ephod, of the same workmanship, with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
They mounted the onyx stones in gold filigree settings, engraved like a seal with the names of the sons of Israel.
Then they fastened them on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel, as the LORD had commanded Moses.
He made the breastpiece with the same workmanship as the ephod, with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen.
It was square when folded over double, a span long and a span wide.
And they mounted on it four rows of gemstones: The first row had a ruby, a topaz, and an emerald;
the second row had a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond;
the third row had a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst;
and the fourth row had a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. These stones were mounted in gold filigree settings.
The twelve stones corresponded to the names of the sons of Israel. Each stone was engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes.
For the breastpiece they made braided chains like cords of pure gold.
They also made two gold filigree settings and two gold rings, and fastened the two rings to the two corners of the breastpiece.
Then they fastened the two gold chains to the two gold rings at the corners of the breastpiece,
and they fastened the other ends of the two chains to the two filigree settings, attaching them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front.
They made two more gold rings and attached them to the other two corners of the breastpiece, on the inside edge next to the ephod.
They made two additional gold rings and attached them to the bottom of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, on its front, near the seam just above its woven waistband.

Then they tied the rings of the breastpiece to the rings of the ephod with a cord of blue yarn, so that the breastpiece was above the waistband of the ephod and would not swing out from the ephod, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

units.label: The robe and remaining garments
units.note: just as the LORD had commanded Moses

verses.text: They made the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth, the work of a weaver,
with an opening in the center of the robe like that of a garment, with a collar around the opening so that it would not tear.
They made pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen on the lower hem of the robe.
They also made bells of pure gold and attached them around the hem between the pomegranates,
alternating the bells and pomegranates around the lower hem of the robe to be worn for ministry, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
For Aaron and his sons they made tunics of fine linen, the work of a weaver,
as well as the turban of fine linen, the ornate headbands and undergarments of finely spun linen,
and the sash of finely spun linen, embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
They also made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and they engraved on it, like an inscription on a seal: {{holy|HOLY TO THE LORD}}.
Then they fastened to it a blue cord to mount it on the turban, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

units.label: Brought to Moses, and blessed
units.note: just as the LORD had commanded

media.alt: A leader inspecting finished tabernacle items
media.caption: Moses inspects all the finished work and blesses the people.

verses.text: So all the work for the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting, was completed. The Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
Then they brought the tabernacle to Moses: the tent with all its furnishings, its clasps, its frames, its crossbars, and its posts and bases;
the covering of ram skins dyed red, the covering of fine leather, and the veil of the covering;
the ark of the Testimony with its poles and the mercy seat;
the table with all its utensils and the Bread of the Presence;
the pure gold lampstand with its row of lamps and all its utensils, as well as the oil for the light;
the gold altar, the anointing oil, the fragrant incense, and the curtain for the entrance to the tent;
the bronze altar with its bronze grating, its poles, and all its utensils; the basin with its stand;

the curtains of the courtyard with its posts and bases; the curtain for the gate of the courtyard, its ropes and tent pegs, and all the equipment for the service of the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting;
and the woven garments for ministering in the sanctuary, both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests.
The Israelites had done all the work just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
And Moses inspected all the work and saw that they had accomplished it just as the LORD had commanded. So Moses {{blessed|blessed}} them.

holy.gloss: Holy to the LORD, engraved on the gold plate worn by Aaron. First commanded in chapter 28, it is here completed exactly as instructed, marking the entire finished project's ultimate purpose: everything set apart wholly for God.

blessed.gloss: To bless, to speak good and favor over someone. Moses' blessing here, after inspecting the completed work, echoes the pattern of blessing that follows faithful completion of God's commands throughout Scripture, most notably at creation itself.

basic.context: The craftsmen finish every priestly garment, ephod, breastpiece, robe, and remaining pieces, exactly as God had commanded, with the phrase 'just as the LORD had commanded Moses' repeated again and again. Everything is then brought to Moses, who personally inspects the entire completed tabernacle and blesses the people for their faithful obedience.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a historical record of exact, careful obedience to earlier divine instruction, not a text requiring symbolic decoding of every detail. Its central theological weight lies in the repeated refrain of obedience and in Moses' concluding inspection and blessing, echoing patterns of completed work and divine approval found elsewhere in Scripture.
basic.originalLanguages: The refrain ka'asher tzivah Yahweh et Mosheh, just as the LORD had commanded Moses, appears repeatedly throughout the chapter, emphasizing precise fidelity to instruction. The gold plate again reads qodesh la-Yahweh, holy to the LORD, and Moses' final act is to barak, bless, the people for their faithful work.
basic.typology: The pattern of completed work followed by inspection and blessing echoes the seventh day of creation, when God saw all that He had made and blessed it. This anticipates the completed work of Christ, who declares 'It is finished' before God's approval is shown in the resurrection, and the pattern of faithful stewardship rewarded that runs throughout Scripture.
basic.christ: Just as Moses inspects the completed tabernacle and finds it done exactly as commanded, God the Father vindicates Christ's finished work of redemption through the resurrection, the ultimate 'well done' spoken over perfectly completed obedience, Hebrews 10:5-10. The repeated phrase of exact obedience here anticipates Christ's own perfect fulfillment of everything the Father commanded.
basic.god: God's detailed commands are met with detailed, faithful obedience, and He responds, through Moses, with blessing, echoing the pattern of creation itself: work completed as commanded leads to divine approval and blessing. God delights not merely in good intentions but in the actual, careful completion of what He has asked.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 1:31-2:3 records God seeing all He had made, declaring it very good, and blessing the seventh day, the pattern this chapter echoes. John 19:30 records Christ's own completed work, 'It is finished.' Matthew 25:21 speaks of the master's 'well done, good and faithful servant.'
basic.oneStory: Israel completes every part of the tabernacle exactly as God commanded, and Moses inspects and blesses the finished work, echoing the pattern of creation completed and blessed. This pattern of faithful completion followed by divine approval reaches its fullest expression in Christ, whose finished work of redemption receives the Father's ultimate approval in the resurrection.

context.literary:
Exodus 39 closes the construction account in two parts. Verses 1 to 31 make the priestly garments, and verses 32 to 43 bring every finished piece to Moses. The first part is marked off by a refrain. 'As the LORD had commanded Moses' closes each stage of the work, in verses 1, 5, 7, 21, 26, 29 and 31, seven times in all. When Moses sets the tabernacle up in the next chapter, the refrain returns another seven times, Exodus 40:19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29 and 32. The number is hardly accidental in a book whose instructions came in seven speeches and closed with the Sabbath.

The order of the garments follows the instructions of chapter 28: ephod, breastpiece, robe, then tunics, turban, headbands, undergarments and sash, and last the gold plate. But the chapter adds something chapter 28 never described: how the gold thread was made. 'They hammered out thin sheets of gold and cut threads from them to interweave' with the yarn, verse 3. The account of execution is not merely a copy of the command; it lets us see the craftsmen at work.

The grammar shifts as well. In chapters 36 to 38 the builder is mostly 'he,' Bezalel at the head of the work. In chapter 39 the verbs are mostly plural, 'they made,' and the summaries twice name the whole nation: 'The Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses,' verse 32, and 'The Israelites had done all the work,' verse 42. The tabernacle is presented as the work of the whole people.

The final paragraph echoes the close of the creation account. 'So all the work... was completed,' verse 32, recalls 'Thus the heavens and the earth were completed,' Genesis 2:1. 'Moses inspected all the work and saw that they had accomplished it,' verse 43, recalls 'God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good,' Genesis 1:31. 'So Moses blessed them,' verse 43, recalls 'Then God blessed the seventh day,' Genesis 2:3. And in the next chapter 'Moses finished the work,' Exodus 40:33, as 'God had finished the work He had been doing,' Genesis 2:2. Between them, verses 33 to 41 list everything brought to Moses in roughly the order it was built, a closing roll call of the whole project.
context.historical:
The ephod was a known type of garment in Israel. Samuel served as a boy 'wearing a linen ephod,' 1 Samuel 2:18, and David danced before the ark in one, 2 Samuel 6:14. Aaron's ephod was far grander, woven of linen, dyed yarn and gold thread, and fitted with shoulder pieces carrying two onyx stones engraved with the twelve names, six on each, 'in the order of their birth,' Exodus 28:10. An ephod could also go wrong: Gideon made one that 'became a snare' when Israel worshiped it, Judges 8:27.

Engraving 'like a seal,' verses 6, 14 and 30, was the craft of cutting names or designs into hard stone or metal, which was well known in the ancient world for signet rings and cylinder seals. Here it put the names of Israel's tribes into gemstones and God's holiness into gold. The BSB footnote on verse 10 notes that the identification of some of the twelve stones is uncertain; the ancient names do not map neatly onto modern gem terms. The breastpiece was square, a span each way when folded double, about nine inches, verse 9.

The robe was solid blue, with an opening 'like that of a garment' bound so that it would not tear, verse 23, where the BSB footnote says the Hebrew term is uncertain and may refer to a coat of mail. Gold bells alternated with pomegranates on the hem so that Aaron's movements would be heard in the sanctuary, Exodus 28:35. Pomegranates later decorated the pillars of Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 7:18. The priests' linen undergarments, verse 28, served modesty at the altar, Exodus 28:42-43.

The work was done within a year of the exodus. Israel reached Sinai in the third month, Exodus 19:1, and the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year, Exodus 40:17, with two periods of forty days on the mountain in between, Exodus 24:18 and 34:28. Moses' inspection and blessing thus fall only a few months after the calf, when the camp had seen judgment and plague, Exodus 32:35.
context.canonical:
The refrain of this chapter carries straight into Leviticus. When Moses ordains Aaron and his sons, each stage ends 'as the LORD had commanded him,' Leviticus 8:9 and 8:13, and the chapter closes, 'So Aaron and his sons did everything the LORD had commanded through Moses,' Leviticus 8:36. Then Aaron lifts his hands and blesses the people, Moses and Aaron bless them together, and 'the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people,' Leviticus 9:22-23. God gives the priests the words for that blessing in Numbers 6:24-26, 'May the LORD bless you and keep you.'

Solomon's temple follows the same pattern. It was 'finished in every detail and according to every specification,' 1 Kings 6:38, and at its dedication Solomon 'blessed the whole assembly of Israel,' saying, 'Not one word has failed of all the good promises He made through His servant Moses,' 1 Kings 8:55-56.

The garments reappear in the prophets. Zechariah sees the high priest Joshua in filthy clothes, which are removed as the angel says, 'I have removed your iniquity, and I will clothe you with splendid robes,' and a clean turban is set on his head, Zechariah 3:3-5. The inscription on the gold plate spreads to ordinary things: 'HOLY TO THE LORD will be inscribed on the bells of the horses,' Zechariah 14:20. Isaiah rejoices that God 'has clothed me with garments of salvation,' Isaiah 61:10.

In the New Testament Hebrews contrasts Moses, 'faithful as a servant in all God's house,' with Christ, 'faithful as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:5-6, and presents Jesus as the great high priest, Hebrews 4:14. John sees the risen Christ 'dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest,' Revelation 1:13, and the new Jerusalem has foundations adorned with precious stones, Revelation 21:19-20, and gates inscribed with the twelve tribes, Revelation 21:12, as though the breastpiece had become a city.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to know that the priesthood which will stand between them and God has been prepared exactly as God required. The garments were not ornaments designed by Aaron's taste. They were made 'to give him glory and splendor,' Exodus 28:2, to God's specification, and every stage is sealed with the refrain of obedience. Israel could trust the high priest who wore them because the clothes themselves bore witness that God had appointed this ministry.

The author also wants the first hearers to see themselves in the garments. Their tribal names were on Aaron's shoulders and over his heart, verses 6 to 14. When the high priest went in before God, the whole people went in with him, remembered and represented.

Finally, the author wants Israel to feel the weight of the moment of verses 42 and 43. After the calf, the people have done 'all the work just as the LORD had commanded Moses.' The mediator who once smashed the tablets now inspects their work and blesses them. The story of Exodus has moved from a people who could not obey to a people who have obeyed, and from God's threat to withdraw, Exodus 33:3, to the eve of His glory filling the tent.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes garments made for Aaron and his sons. It does not tell Christian ministers to wear an ephod or engrave stones, and the New Testament treats the Aaronic priesthood as a shadow fulfilled in Christ, whose priesthood is 'permanent,' Hebrews 7:24. No church office inherits the breastpiece.

What endures is the pattern the chapter displays and the truths the garments carried. God's people are still to do His work as He commands, and the New Testament speaks of believers as 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, who offer spiritual sacrifices 'acceptable to God through Jesus Christ,' 1 Peter 2:5. The call to holiness engraved on the gold plate now rests on every believer. And the blessing of verse 43 reminds leaders that recognizing and blessing faithful work is part of their task, though the chapter does not command a particular form for it.

debates.question: Is the parallel between this chapter's completion and blessing and the creation account in Genesis 1 and 2 an intentional literary device, or a coincidental similarity?

views.label: A deliberate, intentional parallel
views.case: The verbal links are specific. The verb 'completed' in Exodus 39:32 is the one used in Genesis 2:1-2; 'Moses inspected all the work and saw' in verse 43 echoes 'God looked upon all that He had made' in Genesis 1:31; 'Moses blessed them' echoes Genesis 2:3; and 'Moses finished the work,' Exodus 40:33, echoes Genesis 2:2. Add the seven speeches of chapters 25 to 31 ending with the Sabbath, and the sevenfold refrain here and in chapter 40, and many conclude the tabernacle is presented as a renewed creation where God dwells with His people as in Eden.

views.label: A natural similarity of completion accounts
views.case: Others are cautious about pressing the numbers and structure. Any account of a great work finished, checked and approved will share some of this vocabulary, since 'complete,' 'work,' 'see' and 'bless' are common words. On this view the echoes may be real without making the tabernacle a deliberate model of creation.

debates.bearing: The verbal links are close enough that most readers hear Genesis behind Exodus 39 and 40. Even held cautiously, the parallel fits the book's theology: the God who made the world to dwell with humanity now makes a dwelling among His redeemed people.

debates.question: Why are the Urim and Thummim not mentioned among the items the craftsmen made?

views.label: They were not craftsmen's work
views.case: Exodus 28:30 tells Moses to 'place the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece,' but gives no instructions for making them. Chapter 39 records the breastpiece being made and never mentions them, and Leviticus 8:8 has Moses himself place them in it. This suggests they were objects already in existence or supplied in some other way, not products of the workshop.

views.label: They were the stones or part of the breastpiece
views.case: A minority view identifies the Urim and Thummim with the gemstones or with some feature of the breastpiece itself, so they need no separate mention. Against this, Leviticus 8:8 distinguishes them, saying Moses 'put the breastpiece on him and placed the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece.'

debates.bearing: Scripture never describes what the Urim and Thummim looked like, only that they were used to seek God's judgment, Numbers 27:21. Their absence from the craftsmen's list fits the view that they were given rather than made, and it reminds readers that divine guidance was not something Israel's artisans could manufacture.

study.originalLanguages:
The key verb of verse 32 is kalah, to be complete or finished: 'So all the work for the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting, was completed.' It is the verb of Genesis 2:1-2, 'the heavens and the earth were completed' and 'God had finished the work,' and it returns in Exodus 40:33, 'So Moses finished the work.' The word for 'work' in verses 32 and 42 is avodah, a noun that means labour, but also service and worship. The same word covers the craftsmen's weaving and the priests' ministry. In Israel's vocabulary, building God's house and serving Him in it were one kind of activity.

Verse 43 reads literally, 'Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it.' The pairing of 'saw' with 'behold' is exactly the construction of Genesis 1:31, 'God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good.' The narrator lets Moses look at the finished tabernacle the way God looked at the finished world.

The onyx stones on the shoulders are 'memorial stones,' verse 7, from zakar, to remember. Scripture's great turning points often begin with this verb: 'God remembered Noah,' Genesis 8:1, and 'He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,' Exodus 2:24. The stones are not a reminder to Aaron but, as Exodus 28:12 says, 'a memorial before the LORD.' Israel's names were carried into God's presence as a plea that He would remember them.

The breastpiece is the choshen, called in Exodus 28:15 'the breastpiece of judgment,' mishpat, because it held the Urim and Thummim by which God's decisions were sought, Numbers 27:21. The Septuagint rendered the breastpiece logeion, a place of oracle, and translated Urim and Thummim with words meaning manifestation and truth, showing how ancient readers understood it: a garment for receiving God's word.

The 'plate' of verse 30 is the tsits, a word that elsewhere means a flower or blossom, as in 'the flowers fall,' Isaiah 40:7-8, probably because of its shining or ornamental shape. It is called 'the plate of the holy crown.' The noun for crown is nezer, from nazar, to separate or consecrate. It is the word used of the Nazirite, 'because the crown of consecration to his God is upon his head,' Numbers 6:7. On Aaron's forehead sat a crown whose very name meant consecration, engraved with the words that stated it.

The 'bells' of verse 25 are paamon, from a root meaning to strike, and the 'pomegranates' are rimmon, the fruit that later decorated the temple pillars, 1 Kings 7:18. Sound and fruit together ran round the hem of the robe; the sound was so that 'he will not die' when he went in, Exodus 28:35.

Finally, verse 43 ends with 'So Moses blessed them.' Moses does not praise the workers only; he pronounces God's favour over them, as Aaron will soon do in Leviticus 9:22 and as God will give the priests words to do in Numbers 6:24-27.

typology.type: The high priest bearing the tribes' names, Exodus 39:6-14
typology.fulfillment: Aaron carried the twelve names on his shoulders and over his heart whenever he went before the LORD, a continual memorial, Exodus 28:12 and 28:29. Christ is the high priest who 'always lives to intercede' for those who come to God through Him, Hebrews 7:25, and who 'calls his own sheep by name,' John 10:3. God says to Zion, 'I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands,' Isaiah 49:16. The escalation is from names engraved in stone to persons known and loved. The type falls short because Aaron's ministry ended at his death, but Jesus 'lives forever' and 'has a permanent priesthood,' Hebrews 7:24.

typology.type: The gold plate, HOLY TO THE LORD, Exodus 39:30-31
typology.fulfillment: The plate sat on Aaron's forehead so that he might 'bear the iniquity of the holy things' Israel offered, 'so that they may be acceptable before the LORD,' Exodus 28:38. Aaron's engraved holiness covered the imperfection even of Israel's worship. Christ is the high priest who is 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' Hebrews 7:26, and through Him believers offer sacrifices 'acceptable to God,' 1 Peter 2:5. The type falls short because Aaron's holiness was engraved on gold while he himself needed atonement, Hebrews 9:7; Christ's holiness is His own nature.

typology.type: The garments of glory and splendor
typology.fulfillment: Aaron's garments were made 'to give him glory and splendor,' Exodus 28:2, and without them he could not serve. The risen Christ appears 'dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest,' Revelation 1:13, the true High Priest in glory. His people are clothed through Him: those baptized into Christ 'have clothed yourselves with Christ,' Galatians 3:27, and the bride is given 'fine linen, bright and pure,' Revelation 19:8. The type falls short because Aaron's garments could be defiled and passed to another; the righteousness in which believers are clothed is Christ's, and it does not wear out.

typology.type: The completed work, inspected and blessed, Exodus 39:42-43
typology.fulfillment: The people finished the work exactly as commanded, and Moses saw it and blessed them. Jesus says to the Father, 'I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do,' John 17:4, and on the cross, 'It is finished,' John 19:30. Hebrews adds that 'after He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,' Hebrews 1:3. The escalation is that Israel's obedience was dependent and soon broken, while Christ's obedience was complete. The type falls short because the tabernacle would need repair and renewal; His finished work needs neither.

typology.type: Moses, faithful in all God's house
typology.fulfillment: Moses oversees the whole house of God, receives every piece, and confirms that all was done as commanded. Hebrews honours this: 'Moses was faithful as a servant in all God's house, testifying to what would be spoken later,' Hebrews 3:5. But 'Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house. And we are His house,' Hebrews 3:6. The correspondence is faithful oversight of God's dwelling; the escalation is from servant to Son, from a tent of curtains to a house of people. The type falls short because Moses inspected others' work, while Christ is Himself 'the builder of a house,' with 'greater honor than the house itself,' Hebrews 3:3.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the high priest it clothes. Everything in verses 1 to 31 exists so that one man can stand before God on behalf of the people. Hebrews presents Jesus as exactly that: 'we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God,' Hebrews 4:14. Aaron wore the names of the tribes on his shoulders, as a burden carried, and over his heart, as a people loved, Exodus 28:12 and 28:29. Christ bears His people in both ways. He 'always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25, and He is 'able to sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15.

It leads to Christ through the holiness engraved on the plate. Aaron's forehead declared 'HOLY TO THE LORD,' and that holiness made Israel's gifts acceptable, Exodus 28:38. But Aaron himself had to offer for his own sins, Hebrews 9:7. Jesus is the high priest who truly is what the plate proclaimed, 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' Hebrews 7:26, and He needs no sacrifice for Himself.

There is also an echo worth noticing, held carefully because the Gospel does not spell it out. The high priest's robe was woven so that 'it would not tear,' verse 23, and the law forbade the high priest to tear his garments, Leviticus 21:10. At Jesus' trial Caiaphas 'tore his clothes,' Matthew 26:65. At the cross the soldiers found Jesus' tunic 'seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom,' and said, 'Let us not tear it,' John 19:23-24. John's stated point is the fulfillment of Psalm 22, and the priestly echo is at most in the background, but the contrast between the two men is striking.

It leads to Christ through the finished work of verses 42 and 43. Israel completed the tabernacle, and Moses saw and blessed it. Jesus prayed, 'I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do,' John 17:4, and cried from the cross, 'It is finished,' John 19:30. Then the Father raised Him and seated Him at His right hand, Hebrews 1:3. The blessing Moses spoke over completed work is the shadow of the vindication God gave His Son.

It leads to Christ through the contrast between Moses and the Son. Hebrews says Moses was 'faithful as a servant in all God's house,' but Christ is 'faithful as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:5-6. Moses inspected a house of curtains made by others. Christ builds a house of people, 'and we are His house.' When He clothes that house, He clothes it in Himself, Galatians 3:27.

The limits of the typology matter. The New Testament links the priesthood, the garments of glory and the holiness of the high priest to Christ. It does not interpret each gemstone, the number of bells or the colours of the yarn, and a careful reader will let those details stand as what they are, the beauty God commanded for His priest.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who cares about beauty. The garments were made 'to give him glory and splendor,' Exodus 28:2, with gold thread hammered and cut by hand, verse 3, and twelve engraved stones. God is not indifferent to form. The One who made a world full of colour asks that His priest be dressed with artistry, and He supplies the skill for it through the Spirit, Exodus 31:3.

It shows a God who remembers. The stones on Aaron's shoulders are 'memorial stones,' verse 7, carried 'as a memorial before the LORD,' Exodus 28:12. God does not need reminding, yet He appoints signs by which His people may know they are remembered. From Noah, Genesis 8:1, to Israel in Egypt, Exodus 2:24, God's remembering means God acting in faithfulness. The names on the high priest's heart are a promise that God keeps His people before Him.

It shows the holiness of God. The inscription 'HOLY TO THE LORD' stands on the most visible part of the priest, on his forehead. Holiness is not an ornament of Israel's worship; it is its point. The bells ring 'so that he will not die,' Exodus 28:35, and the undergarments are worn 'so that they will not incur guilt and die,' Exodus 28:43. God is gracious to let a man come near, but He remains the Holy One, and nearness has conditions He sets.

It shows a God who guides His people. The breastpiece of judgment held the means by which Israel sought God's decisions, Numbers 27:21. The God of Exodus does not leave His people to guess; He speaks, and He has appointed ways for His will to be known.

It shows a God who delights in obedience and blesses it. The repeated refrain, 'as the LORD had commanded Moses,' is not the language of a tyrant satisfied that his orders were followed. It ends in blessing, verse 43. God's commands are for His people's good, and completed obedience opens the way for His presence, which fills the tabernacle in the next chapter, Exodus 40:34. This echoes creation, when God finished His work and blessed, Genesis 2:3: the God who works also rests and blesses.

It shows a God who restores. Only months earlier this people had worshiped a calf and been told God might not go with them, Exodus 33:3. Now their work is finished and blessed. The God who judged the sin has forgiven the sinners and accepted their work.

For worship, the chapter calls for holiness, gratitude and confidence. Believers are now 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, and the words of Aaron's plate are meant to be true of all God's people, Zechariah 14:20-21. They come to God not in Aaron's garments but in Christ, whose righteousness clothes them and whose finished work has already received the Father's blessing.

crossReferences.note: The instructions for the priestly garments that Exodus 39:1-31 carries out. Chapter 28 gives the purposes, glory and splendor, memorial, judgment, bearing iniquity, while chapter 39 records the making in the same order, adding details such as how the gold thread was cut from hammered sheets.

Moses clothes Aaron in the garments made in Exodus 39, tunic, sash, robe, ephod, breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, turban and gold plate, 'as the LORD had commanded him.' The refrain of Exodus 39 continues into the ordination, linking the making of the garments to their use.

Aaron lifts his hands and blesses the people, then Moses and Aaron bless them together, and the glory of the LORD appears and fire consumes the offering. The blessing Moses gave in Exodus 39:43 becomes the pattern of priestly ministry, followed by the visible approval of God.

The heavens and earth 'were completed,' God 'finished the work,' and God 'blessed the seventh day.' Exodus 39:32 and 39:43, with Exodus 40:33, use the same vocabulary for the tabernacle, presenting God's dwelling among Israel as a new beginning echoing the first creation.

God gives Aaron and his sons the words of blessing: 'May the LORD bless you and keep you.' Moses' blessing in Exodus 39:43 anticipates this priestly blessing, by which the priests 'put My name on the Israelites,' just as Aaron wore God's name on his forehead.

The high priest Joshua stands in filthy garments; they are removed, and he is given splendid robes and a clean turban, with the words, 'I have removed your iniquity.' The garments of Exodus 39 become a picture of a priesthood cleansed and restored by God's grace.

On that day 'HOLY TO THE LORD' will be inscribed on the bells of horses, and every pot in Jerusalem will be holy. The words engraved on Aaron's gold plate in Exodus 39:30 spread to the whole of life, showing that the holiness of the priest was meant to fill the people.

The prophet rejoices that God 'has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress.' The priestly garments of Exodus 39 supply the imagery for God's gift of salvation to His people.

Moses was faithful as a servant in all God's house, but Christ is faithful as the Son over it, 'and we are His house.' Exodus 39:32-43 shows Moses' faithful oversight of God's house; Hebrews shows the greater Son to whom that faithfulness pointed.

'Such a high priest truly befits us, One who is holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners.' What Aaron's gold plate declared by engraving, Christ is by nature, and He needs no sacrifice for Himself, unlike the priest dressed in the garments of Exodus 39.

Jesus says, 'It is finished,' and yields up His spirit. The completion of the tabernacle in Exodus 39:32 and 39:42 foreshadows the completion of Christ's work, by which the true dwelling of God with humanity is secured.

The foundations of the new Jerusalem are adorned with twelve precious stones, several of which share names with the stones of the breastpiece in English translation. The city itself carries what the high priest once wore, the people of God set in glory before Him.

In the new creation God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads.' What only Aaron wore, the name of the LORD on the forehead, is given to every servant of God in the city where He dwells.

study.oneStory:
Clothing has been part of the Bible's story since the garden. Before the fall the man and woman were naked and unashamed; after it they sewed fig leaves, and then 'the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them,' Genesis 3:21. The first clothing God gave covered shame. In Exodus 39 God clothes a man again, this time not merely to cover him but to give him 'glory and splendor,' Exodus 28:2, so that he can stand before God on behalf of others.

Adam was placed in the garden 'to cultivate and keep it,' Genesis 2:15, and the same pair of verbs later describes the Levites' duties at the tabernacle, Numbers 3:7-8. Many readers see Adam as a kind of first priest in the first sanctuary. What he lost, access to God's presence and a calling to serve there, is here given back in a limited form to Aaron, and through him to a nation called to be 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation,' Exodus 19:6.

The Old Testament shows how fragile this priesthood was. Aaron's sons offered unauthorized fire and died, Leviticus 10:1-2. Eli's sons corrupted the sanctuary, and by Malachi's day the priests had 'violated the covenant of Levi,' Malachi 2:8. The prophets looked for a cleansed priest in clean garments, Zechariah 3:3-5, and a day when everything would be holy to the LORD, Zechariah 14:20.

That day dawns in Christ, the high priest who is holy by nature, Hebrews 7:26, who finished the work the Father gave Him, John 17:4, and who now clothes His people in Himself, Galatians 3:27. Through Him the church becomes 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, and a people made to be 'priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:6.

The story ends where the gold plate points. In the new Jerusalem the redeemed wear robes 'washed' and 'made white in the blood of the Lamb,' Revelation 7:14. The city's foundations shine with precious stones, Revelation 21:19-20, and its gates bear the names of the twelve tribes, Revelation 21:12, like the stones Aaron carried on his shoulders and heart. And in that city God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4. What once was engraved on one priest's forehead, HOLY TO THE LORD, will be written on all God's people, and the work God began will be finished and blessed forever.

quiz.q: What phrase is repeated throughout this chapter to describe how the priestly garments were made?

options.text: Just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
options.note: This exact refrain appears repeatedly, including in verses 1, 5, 7, 21, 26, 29, and 31.

options.text: According to the wisdom of the elders.
options.note: The repeated refrain specifically credits the LORD's command through Moses, not the elders' independent wisdom.

options.text: As Bezalel personally preferred.
options.note: The emphasis throughout is on obedience to God's command, not Bezalel's personal preference.

options.text: No refrain is repeated in this chapter.
options.note: The phrase just as the LORD had commanded Moses is explicitly repeated multiple times.

quiz.q: What did the twelve stones on the breastpiece represent, according to verse 14?

options.text: The names of the twelve tribes of Israel, one stone per tribe.
options.note: Verse 14 states this correspondence explicitly.

options.text: The twelve months of the Hebrew calendar.
options.note: The stones correspond to the twelve tribes, not a calendar system.

options.text: The twelve plagues brought upon Egypt.
options.note: There were ten plagues, not twelve, and the stones represent the tribes, not the plagues.

options.text: No meaning is given for the twelve stones.
options.note: Verse 14 explicitly explains the stones represent the twelve tribes.

quiz.q: What was engraved on the gold plate of the holy crown, according to verse 30?

options.text: HOLY TO THE LORD.
options.note: Verse 30 gives this exact inscription, matching the original command in chapter 28.

options.text: The names of Moses and Aaron.
options.note: The inscription is a declaration of holiness to the LORD, not the names of Moses and Aaron.

options.text: The Ten Commandments in full.
options.note: The commandments were on the stone tablets, not engraved on this gold plate.

options.text: No inscription is mentioned.
options.note: Verse 30 explicitly gives the inscription: Holy to the LORD.

quiz.q: What did Moses do after inspecting all the completed work, according to verse 43?

options.text: He blessed the people.
options.note: Verse 43 states this exact response after his inspection.

options.text: He ordered the work redone from scratch.
options.note: The text states the work matched every command exactly, so nothing needed to be redone; Moses blessed the people instead.

options.text: He remained silent and said nothing.
options.note: Verse 43 explicitly records Moses' blessing, not silence.

options.text: He rebuked the people for delays.
options.note: The text records approval and blessing, not rebuke, since the work matched every command.

quiz.q: What conclusion does verse 43 draw about how the Israelites had completed the work?

options.text: They had accomplished it just as the LORD had commanded.
options.note: Verse 43 states this exact conclusion, prompting Moses' blessing.

options.text: They had completed only half of what was required.
options.note: The verse specifically affirms complete, exact fulfillment of every command, not a partial completion.

options.text: They had substituted their own preferred designs.
options.note: The verse emphasizes exact conformity to the LORD's command, not personal substitution or preference.

options.text: No evaluation of the work is given.
options.note: Verse 43 explicitly evaluates the work as accomplished just as the LORD commanded.

questions: The repeated phrase 'just as the LORD had commanded Moses' marks every stage of this work. Where in your own obedience do you tend to settle for approximate faithfulness rather than careful, exact obedience to what God has asked?

Moses personally inspected every piece before blessing the people, taking the time to verify careful completion. How do you respond when your own work or service is closely examined, with defensiveness or openness?

The blessing came only after the work matched God's command exactly, echoing the pattern of creation completed and blessed. Where do you look for approval, from finishing well according to God's standard, or from other measures of success?

The gold plate reading 'Holy to the LORD' had been commanded back in chapter 28 and is only now, after much patient work, actually completed and worn. What long-obeyed but not yet finished commitment in your own life needs patient follow-through to completion?

This whole massive project, after the disaster of the golden calf, ends in blessing rather than further judgment. Where do you need hope that faithful obedience today can be part of God restoring what was broken by past failure?

translationNotes.note: The phrase just as the LORD had commanded Moses recurs so consistently through this chapter, appearing at least seven times, that many scholars see it as a deliberate structural echo of the sevenfold pattern of divine speeches and completion language in Genesis 1.

The tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting was completed uses both names for the structure together, emphasizing that the physical building work, and the purpose of meeting with God it was built for, were both now fully realized.

Moses blessed them echoes the same verb, barak, used of God blessing the completed work of creation in Genesis 2:3, reinforcing the tabernacle's presentation as a kind of new creation where God will dwell among His people.
